blocks: Duration and frequency follow the training plan. Begin with a duration that ends with energy left over, then add a few minutes in weeks that feel comfortable, keeping the pace conversational.

Successful practice feels steady and repeatable from start to finish. Pain that changes your stride, or breathing too hard to speak, means slow to a walk. Brisk walking, cycling, or the elliptical at the same effort can substitute.
Person/Andrew Huberman/Book/26/Protocols places a long, steady endurance session on Day 1 of the weekly plan.
Practice short hard efforts on a stationary bike or rower, separated by easy recovery.
Use a stationary bike or rower with a familiar setup. Warm up for 5–10 minutes, finishing with a few brief pickups in effort.

One round is a hard effort followed by easy movement. Drive the pedals or the stroke hard for the work period while keeping posture and form, then reduce to easy movement until breathing settles. Finish the session with about five minutes of easy movement.

Work length, recovery length, effort, and rounds follow the training plan. Start below all-out effort with fewer rounds; add rounds before raising effort, and only while the other workouts and recovery remain good.
Each hard effort should be repeatable at about the same power or pace. A fading final round, or legs tired enough to change movement, means stopping early or switching to easy cardio for the day.
Person/Andrew Huberman/Book/26/Protocols places 6–12 near-all-out intervals on Day 6 of the weekly plan.
Practice continuous moderate-effort cardio on a bike or elliptical, breathing harder while keeping the pace sustainable.
Adjust the bike saddle so the knee stays slightly bent at the bottom of the pedal stroke, or set the elliptical stride and resistance to a smooth motion. Warm up easily for about five minutes.
Raise resistance or cadence until breathing is noticeably harder and speech is limited to short phrases. Hold that effort without fading for the planned duration, then ease off for a few minutes.
Duration follows the training plan. Lengthen the session a few minutes at a time while the effort stays sustainable from start to finish.
The final minutes should feel like the first ones. Gasping or a slowing cadence means the effort is too high. A rower, brisk incline walk, or easy jog at the same effort can substitute.
Person/Andrew Huberman/Book/26/Protocols places a moderate cardio session of 25–30 minutes on Day 5 of the weekly plan.
Practice walking at an easy to brisk pace to add daily movement and support recovery.
Wear comfortable shoes and choose a route, hallway, or treadmill.
Walk upright with a natural arm swing. An easy walk allows relaxed conversation; a brisk walk raises breathing while conversation remains possible.
Walk for five to ten minutes after meals when practical, and take a short walk during long periods of sitting or standing. Build daily steps gradually from the current average.
Walking should leave you fresher, not more tired. Shorter, more frequent walks work when time or energy is limited.
Person/Andrew Huberman/Book/26/Protocols suggests five minutes of walking per half-hour of sitting, walks after meals, and roughly 7,000–10,000 daily steps.
Practice raising the arms with the forearms pressed together while holding a hip hinge, opening the upper back and shoulders.

Stand in a Exercise/Body/Flexibility/Founder Pose with the hips back and the chest lifted. Bring the arms in front of you with the elbows bent at 90 degrees, forearms touching and palms and fingers pressed together.
Keep the forearms together and raise them as high as you can through a full range, then lower them. The set ends when the elbows separate.
The video does two sets of 10 to 15 lifts. If full repetitions are too hard, press up once and hold the squeeze.
Squeeze each finger, the palms, and the elbows together the whole time; the exercise stops working when the elbows come apart.
Demonstration: Eric Goodman's elbow-squeeze arm raise, 10:00. Full notes: Person/Andrew Huberman/Book/26/Protocols/YouTube/11/07/Original 12 Minutes of Foundation Training.
Practice a long-spine hip hinge with a comfortable arm reach and steady breathing.
Stand with feet a little wider than shoulder width and knees softly bent. Hinge at the hips so the hips move backward and the torso inclines forward.
Lengthen through the spine, lift the chest, and raise the arms only as far as you can while keeping the position comfortable. Breathe and exhale slowly, then return to standing.
Begin with a shallow hinge and a few calm breaths, then stand to reset. Add reach or hinge depth gradually while keeping the spine controlled.
Begin with a shallow hinge and a few slow breaths. Keep the arms lower if raising them makes the back arch or the shoulders uncomfortable.
Demonstration: Huberman's Founder pose, 5:15. Full notes: Person/Andrew Huberman/Book/26/Protocols/YouTube/26/09/Mobility and Flexibility.
Demonstration: Eric Goodman's founder, 0:00. Full notes: Person/Andrew Huberman/Book/26/Protocols/YouTube/11/07/Original 12 Minutes of Foundation Training.
Practice loading the femur into the hip socket on hands and knees to restore internal and external hip rotation.
Kneel on all fours with the working knee under the hip at 90 degrees of hip flexion. Draw the knee toward the midline to wind up the hip capsule.

Push your weight back through the femur toward the back of the hip, then glide sideways without dropping to the ground, keeping that line of force. From there add a little more flexion or rotation, move the pelvis and torso on the femur, or use the other leg to press the working leg into internal or external rotation.
About two minutes per side, per the video. Assess rotation before and after.

Aim for a rotation window of 75 to 90 degrees with the femur vertical and loaded, about 45 degrees external and 30 degrees internal. If the front of the hip pinches, loop a band around the upper thigh and anchor it to the side or behind you to pull the femur slightly out of the socket.
Demonstration: Kelly Starrett's joint capsule mobilization, 5:30. Full notes: Person/Andrew Huberman/Book/26/Protocols/YouTube/20/05/If Your Hip Doesn't Rotate You Can't Be at Full Power.
Practice a controlled hip-extension position that stretches the front of the rear hip.
In a split stance or half-kneeling lunge, place one leg behind the body and keep the pelvis facing forward. Use support for balance or padding under the rear knee.

Gently move the pelvis forward while keeping the trunk tall and the low back comfortable. Aim for a stretch at the front of the rear hip. Raising the same-side arm can add to the movement, provided the back remains controlled.
Begin with 10–30 seconds per side and repeat as comfortable. Add range gradually while keeping the low back comfortable.
Begin with 10–30 seconds per side and repeat as comfortable. A shorter stance and smaller movement are useful starting versions. Avoid creating the stretch only by arching the lower back.
Demonstration: Huberman's hip-extension stretch, 2:15. Full notes: Person/Andrew Huberman/Book/26/Protocols/YouTube/26/09/Mobility and Flexibility.
Demonstration: Eric Goodman's lunge stretch, 2:37. Full notes: Person/Andrew Huberman/Book/26/Protocols/YouTube/11/07/Original 12 Minutes of Foundation Training.
Practice moving into a supported shoulder-extension position while raising the hips.
Sit with knees bent, feet flat, and hands behind the hips, fingers pointing outward. Press through hands and feet to raise the hips toward a tabletop position.
Keep the neck comfortable and breathe. Lift only as high as your shoulders and wrists comfortably allow; begin with short holds and lower under control.
Begin with short holds and work toward a comfortable ten-second hold. Increase height or try the next shoulder-extension variation only while the position remains comfortable.
Work toward a comfortable ten-second hold before trying the video's further shoulder-extension progressions. Keep a lower hip position or a shorter hold if full height is not comfortable.
Demonstration: Huberman's reverse tabletop, 3:41. Full notes: Person/Andrew Huberman/Book/26/Protocols/YouTube/26/09/Mobility and Flexibility.
Practice upper-body rotation while maintaining a comfortable wide squat.
Take a wide stance with toes turned slightly outward. Lower into a comfortable squat with the feet grounded, then place the elbows lightly against the inner knees.

Keep one elbow supported while raising the other arm and turning the upper body to follow the hand with the eyes. Return to the center and change sides. Point diagonally upward if reaching the ceiling is uncomfortable.
Begin with three slow turns per side, pausing briefly and breathing. Add range gradually while keeping the squat stable.
Start with three slow turns per side, pausing briefly and breathing. Use a shallower squat or hold a stable support when the bottom position is difficult.
Demonstration: Huberman's sumo squat with rotation, 0:28. Full notes: Person/Andrew Huberman/Book/26/Protocols/YouTube/26/09/Mobility and Flexibility.
Practice a split-stance hip hinge that loads the front glute and hamstring while the back stays braced.
Stand with one foot forward and one back, feet pointing the same way and hips square. Bend the front knee slightly and keep it behind the ankle.

Brace the spine, push the hips back, and press the chest forward until the front hamstring stretches. Reach the arms forward and up and hold. Then cross the arms over the chest and hinge up and down, moving the upper body as one unit from the front hip.
The video holds the reach briefly, adds a rotation toward the front leg as 10 to 15 repetitions or a static hold, then does 8 to 10 hinges per side.
Press through the front heel and keep the front knee from sliding forward. Any bend in the lower back means the hinge has gone too far.
Demonstration: Eric Goodman's split-stance hinge, 3:31. Full notes: Person/Andrew Huberman/Book/26/Protocols/YouTube/11/07/Original 12 Minutes of Foundation Training.
Practice lowering and raising the torso from a hip-hinged position on a hyperextension bench to train the lower back and hip extensors.
Day 4 at 10:30 in Person/Andrew Huberman/Book/26/Protocols/YouTube/26/09/Day 4 - Major Torso Muscles
Day 4 at 11:24 in Person/Andrew Huberman/Book/26/Protocols/YouTube/26/09/Day 4 - Major Torso Muscles

Adjust a hyperextension (45-degree or horizontal) bench so the pad sits just below the hip crease and the heels are secured under the ankle rollers. Start with the body in a straight line, hands crossed on the chest or behind the head.

Bend at the hips to lower the torso slowly toward the floor, then raise it back until the body is in a straight line again. Stop at a straight line rather than arching the lower back past it. Each repetition is slow and controlled.
Huberman suggests 8 to 25 controlled repetitions per set and does about 100 repetitions a week. Add load by holding a plate or dumbbell at the chest or by anchoring a band under the bench.

Reduce the range or remove the added load if the movement turns into a swing or the lower back pinches at the top. Without a machine, hold the edge of a high countertop or sturdy table with the torso supported and lift the legs behind you.
